A0485.explanation: Landlords, sellers, and rental agents may use reasonable applicant-selection standards only if applied equally and uniformly to all applicants. Tenant selection may be based on an applicant’s ability to pay rent, care for the apartment, and respect others’ rights. Housing discrimination based on protected categories, including source of income, is prohibited.

Cities and towns may not enact, maintain, or enforce rent control, except a city or town that accepts Chapter 40P may adopt rent control subject to the stated conditions, including voluntary and uncoerced owner compliance after six months, limits on what the regulation may cover, and municipal compensation to affected owners.

A person furnishing rental accommodations may not discriminate against an individual because the individual receives public assistance or a housing subsidy, including rental assistance or rental supplements.

Covered housing providers may not refuse to rent or lease housing, or discriminate in its terms, conditions, privileges, facilities, or services, because a person has children who occupy or will occupy the premises.

For nonpayment of rent due under a written lease, a landlord may determine the lease by giving the tenant 14 days’ written notice to quit. The tenant may prevent termination by paying or tendering all rent due, with interest and costs, by the specified deadline in a possession action. Special continuance and notice procedures apply when nonpayment was caused by a government payment delay.

Either party may terminate an estate at will by written notice of three months, or, when rent is payable at intervals shorter than three months, by notice equal to the payment interval or 30 days, whichever is longer. For nonpayment, a landlord may give 14 days’ written notice to quit. If the tenant has not received a similar notice in the preceding 12 months, the tenant may prevent termination by paying or tendering all rent due within 10 days after receipt; the notice must inform the tenant of this right.

At or before the start of a tenancy, a lessor or the lessor’s agent may require a security deposit no greater than the first month’s rent. The deposit remains the tenant’s property and must be held in a separate, interest-bearing account. The statute also sets requirements for receipts, interest, return of the deposit, and permitted deductions.

When the lessor transfers an interest in the property, the security deposit and accrued interest must be transferred to the successor in interest. The successor must notify the tenant in writing within 45 days, including the specified contact information, and is liable for retaining and returning the deposit under the section. If the deposit is not transferred, the successor generally assumes liability; for an occupying tenant, the successor may satisfy the obligation by providing equivalent free use and occupancy.

A lessor forfeits the right to retain any part of the security deposit for specified violations, including failure to hold the funds as required, transfer the deposit as required, or return the amount due within 30 days after tenancy ends. For failures to comply with the specified deposit-account, transfer, or return requirements, the tenant is entitled to three times the deposit or balance due, 5% interest from when payment became due, court costs, and reasonable attorney's fees.

When a lessor transfers an interest in a dwelling unit after receiving rent in advance for the last month of tenancy, the lessor must credit the advance and accrued interest to the successor. The successor is liable for crediting the tenant and paying accrued interest, and must provide written notice within 45 days containing the specified information.

A notice of termination of tenancy (other than for nonpayment of rent) within six months after a tenant engages in specified protected activity creates a rebuttable presumption of reprisal. The presumption may be rebutted only by clear and convincing evidence that the action was not retaliatory and had sufficient independent justification.

If a tenant provides a reusable screening report, the landlord must use it.

A landlord cannot charge a screening fee when no rental unit is available. The landlord must return the fee to an applicant not selected, unless the landlord follows the stated application-order and no-charge-for-unconsidered-applicants policy.

Starting July 1, 2024, many landlords may charge no more than one month’s rent for furnished or unfurnished units. Landlords meeting the stated small-owner and ownership conditions may charge up to two months’ rent.
Last month’s rent is considered part of the security deposit; first month’s rent is not.
For a tenancy beginning on or after July 1, 2025, the landlord must photograph the unit immediately before or at the start of the tenancy to document its condition.
The landlord must offer a walk-through inspection during the last two weeks of a tenancy to identify items needing repair or cleaning.

A landlord may deduct only amounts reasonably necessary for rent default, tenant- or guest-caused damage beyond normal wear and tear, qualifying cleaning, and—if allowed by the lease—restoring or replacing personal property or furniture, excluding ordinary wear and tear.

A landlord may not require payment for, or claim against the tenant or deposit for, professional carpet cleaning or other professional cleaning unless reasonably necessary to return the premises to its starting condition, minus ordinary wear and tear.

The landlord must return the deposit or remaining portion within 21 days after the tenant leaves the unit vacant. If deductions are made, the landlord must provide a written itemized statement and supporting documents for repair or cleaning charges; starting January 1, 2025, the landlord must also provide proof that necessary repairs were completed.

Starting April 1, 2025, the landlord must photograph the unit after regaining possession but before repairs or cleaning for which a deposit deduction is intended. The photographs and a written explanation of the cost must be provided to the tenant with the itemized statement.
Housing providers may not charge households with children a higher security deposit as a discriminatory condition or rule.
Tenant screening, including screening conducted by a third party, may not discriminate based on a protected characteristic.

Housing providers may not discriminate against applicants or tenants based on their source of income, including by applying different tenancy terms or charging a higher security deposit because of that source.

Housing providers may not consider arrests that did not lead to conviction, sealed or expunged records, or juvenile-system matters, and may not impose blanket bans on people with criminal history. A conviction used to deny an application must be directly related to the applicant’s ability to be a good tenant and not threaten health, safety, or property; consider the crime’s nature and severity and time elapsed.

Prohibits using or distributing a common pricing algorithm as part of a contract, combination, or conspiracy to restrain trade or commerce, and prohibits using or distributing one to coerce another person to set or adopt its recommended price or commercial term.

For residential property used as the tenant’s dwelling, a landlord generally may not demand or receive security exceeding one month’s rent, in addition to first-month rent. A qualifying small landlord may demand up to two months’ rent, subject to the service-member limitation. An advance payment of at least six months’ rent is permitted when the lease term is six months or longer.

If a landlord or agent charges a service member higher-than-standard or higher-than-advertised security because of credit history, credit score, housing history, or another tenant-related factor, the landlord must provide a written statement of the amount and reason by the lease-signing date. The additional security must be returned after no more than six months of residency if the tenant is not in arrears for rent during that period, and the lease must state the return date.

A landlord may claim from security only amounts reasonably necessary for the purposes specified in subdivision (b). The landlord may not charge for preexisting damage or defective conditions, ordinary wear and tear, or professional cleaning unless reasonably necessary to return the premises to their inception-of-tenancy condition, excluding ordinary wear and tear.

After notice of an intention to terminate the tenancy or before the lease ends, the landlord must notify the tenant in writing of the option to request an initial inspection and the right to attend. If requested, the landlord must conduct the inspection at a reasonable time no earlier than two weeks before termination or lease end, and provide an itemized statement of proposed repair or cleaning deductions.
For tenancies that begin on or after July 1, 2025, the landlord must take photographs of the unit immediately before or at the inception of the tenancy.

Beginning April 1, 2025, the landlord must photograph the unit within a reasonable time after possession is returned and before repairs or cleaning for which a security deduction or claim will be made, and again within a reasonable time after those repairs or cleaning are completed.

No later than 21 calendar days after the tenant vacates, the landlord must provide an itemized statement of the basis for and amount of security received and its disposition, and return any remaining security, subject to the section’s timing and return-method provisions.
Security must be held by the landlord for the tenant who is party to the lease or agreement, and the tenant’s claim to the security takes priority over claims of the landlord’s creditors.

When deducting for repairs or cleaning, a landlord generally must provide supporting documentation with the itemized statement. If the work is done by the landlord or an employee, the statement must describe the work, time spent, and reasonable hourly rate. For work performed by others, the landlord must provide the bill, invoice, or receipt and, when needed, the provider’s contact information. Material costs and applicable photographs and cost explanations must also be provided. A good-faith estimate may be used in specified circumstances, with follow-up documentation due within 14 calendar days after the repair is completed or documentation is received.

When a landlord’s interest in the premises terminates, the landlord or agent must within a reasonable time either transfer the remaining security, after lawful deductions, to the successor in interest and notify the tenant of the transfer and relevant details, or return the remaining security to the tenant with an accounting. Before a voluntary transfer, the landlord must provide the successor a written statement of the remaining security, deductions, and election.

A lease or rental agreement may not characterize security as nonrefundable. Bad-faith claiming or retaining security in violation of the section, or bad-faith demand for replacement security in violation of the section, may result in statutory damages of up to twice the security amount in addition to actual damages.

A landlord may charge an application screening fee only up to the actual out-of-pocket costs and reasonable value of time spent obtaining applicant information, and the fee may not exceed $30 per applicant, subject to annual CPI adjustment.

A landlord may not charge an application screening fee when they know or should know that no rental unit is available now or within a reasonable time. A fee may be charged only when the landlord offers a qualifying screening process: completed applications considered in received order under written criteria, with the first applicant meeting those criteria approved and fees charged only when an application is considered; or the entire fee is returned to applicants not selected within the specified deadline. The landlord must provide an itemized receipt and return any unused portion of the fee when specified screening services are not performed.

A housing provider may not use a financial or income standard that fails to count the aggregate income of people residing or proposing to reside together on the same basis as the aggregate income of married people living together.
The ordinance protects residents with arrest or conviction history in affordable housing decisions.

A landlord may evict a tenant from a rental unit covered by the Rent Ordinance only for a just-cause reason that is the dominant motive for the eviction. The document summarizes 17 just-cause reasons under Ordinance Section 37.9(a).
For rent-controlled units, the annual allowable rent increase is limited to 1.6% for the stated period.
Prohibits the sale or use of algorithmic devices to set rents or manage occupancy levels for residential units in San Francisco.

For notices served from March 1, 2026 through February 28, 2027, relocation payments are $8,245 per tenant, capped at $24,733 per unit, plus $5,497 for each elderly or disabled tenant or household with minor children.

For Ellis Act eviction notices served from March 1, 2026 through February 28, 2027, relocation payments are $11,110.05 per tenant, capped at $33,330.13 per unit, plus $7,443.90 for each elderly or disabled tenant.

A0488.explanation: A person furnishing rental accommodations may not discriminate against an individual because the individual receives public assistance or a housing subsidy, including rental assistance or rental supplements.

For nonpayment of rent due under a written lease, a landlord may determine the lease by giving the tenant 14 days’ written notice to quit. The tenant may prevent termination by paying or tendering all rent due, with interest and costs, by the specified deadline in a possession action. Special continuance and notice procedures apply when nonpayment was caused by a government payment delay.

Either party may terminate an estate at will by written notice of three months, or, when rent is payable at intervals shorter than three months, by notice equal to the payment interval or 30 days, whichever is longer. For nonpayment, a landlord may give 14 days’ written notice to quit. If the tenant has not received a similar notice in the preceding 12 months, the tenant may prevent termination by paying or tendering all rent due within 10 days after receipt; the notice must inform the tenant of this right.

At or before the start of a tenancy, a lessor or the lessor’s agent may require a security deposit no greater than the first month’s rent. The deposit remains the tenant’s property and must be held in a separate, interest-bearing account. The statute also sets requirements for receipts, interest, return of the deposit, and permitted deductions.

When the lessor transfers an interest in the property, the security deposit and accrued interest must be transferred to the successor in interest. The successor must notify the tenant in writing within 45 days, including the specified contact information, and is liable for retaining and returning the deposit under the section. If the deposit is not transferred, the successor generally assumes liability; for an occupying tenant, the successor may satisfy the obligation by providing equivalent free use and occupancy.

A lessor forfeits the right to retain any part of the security deposit for specified violations, including failure to hold the funds as required, transfer the deposit as required, or return the amount due within 30 days after tenancy ends. For failures to comply with the specified deposit-account, transfer, or return requirements, the tenant is entitled to three times the deposit or balance due, 5% interest from when payment became due, court costs, and reasonable attorney's fees.

When a lessor transfers an interest in a dwelling unit after receiving rent in advance for the last month of tenancy, the lessor must credit the advance and accrued interest to the successor. The successor is liable for crediting the tenant and paying accrued interest, and must provide written notice within 45 days containing the specified information.

A notice of termination of tenancy (other than for nonpayment of rent) within six months after a tenant engages in specified protected activity creates a rebuttable presumption of reprisal. The presumption may be rebutted only by clear and convincing evidence that the action was not retaliatory and had sufficient independent justification.

A0489.explanation: Before accepting any application fee, a housing provider must disclose in writing whether its eligibility criteria include review and consideration of criminal history, and inform the applicant that they may provide evidence of inaccuracies, rehabilitation, or other mitigating factors.

A housing provider may not knowingly or purposefully publish a housing advertisement stating that it will not consider any applicant who has been arrested or convicted of one or more crimes or offenses, except for the statutory exceptions. The Act also restricts discriminatory statements, inquiries, and use or dissemination of an applicant’s criminal record.
A housing provider may not require an applicant to submit to a drug or alcohol test or request consent to obtain information from a drug abuse treatment facility.

After finding that a housing provider violated the act, the director may require the provider to return the applicant’s rental application fee, unless housing is provided to the applicant under paragraph (2).
A landlord may not evict a tenant solely because the lease term has ended.

When a tenant terminates a lease under the Safe Housing Act, the landlord must make the security deposit and interest available within 15 business days after termination. The landlord must notify the tenant in writing within three business days of when and where to collect it, and keep it available for 30 days. Any deductions must be itemized.
A landlord may not collect a security deposit exceeding one and one-half times one month’s rent. A pet security deposit counts toward that combined limit.
Any additional yearly security deposit increase may not exceed 10% of the current security deposit.

Interest or earnings on the security deposit belong to the tenant and must be paid in cash or credited toward rent on the lease renewal or anniversary, or on January 31 if the tenant received written notice that payment will be made annually on that date.

Within 30 days after the tenancy ends, the landlord must return the security deposit plus interest earned, less lawful deductions. Any deductions require an itemized list sent to the tenant by registered or certified mail within that 30-day period.

Within five business days after a tenant is displaced by fire, flood, condemnation, or evacuation, the landlord must return the security deposit if an authorized public official has posted a notice prohibiting occupancy or certified that displacement is expected to last longer than seven days. The landlord must tell the tenant within three business days after receiving notice where the deposit can be collected.
A landlord may charge a prospective tenant the cost of a credit report and may request reasonable rental application fees or employment verification.

A0495.explanation: Before accepting any application fee, a housing provider must disclose in writing whether its eligibility criteria include review and consideration of criminal history, and inform the applicant that they may provide evidence of inaccuracies, rehabilitation, or other mitigating factors.

A housing provider may not knowingly or purposefully publish a housing advertisement stating that it will not consider any applicant who has been arrested or convicted of one or more crimes or offenses, except for the statutory exceptions. The Act also restricts discriminatory statements, inquiries, and use or dissemination of an applicant’s criminal record.
A housing provider may not require an applicant to submit to a drug or alcohol test or request consent to obtain information from a drug abuse treatment facility.

After finding that a housing provider violated the act, the director may require the provider to return the applicant’s rental application fee, unless housing is provided to the applicant under paragraph (2).
A landlord may not evict a tenant solely because the lease term has ended.

When a tenant terminates a lease under the Safe Housing Act, the landlord must make the security deposit and interest available within 15 business days after termination. The landlord must notify the tenant in writing within three business days of when and where to collect it, and keep it available for 30 days. Any deductions must be itemized.
A landlord may not collect a security deposit exceeding one and one-half times one month’s rent. A pet security deposit counts toward that combined limit.
Any additional yearly security deposit increase may not exceed 10% of the current security deposit.

Interest or earnings on the security deposit belong to the tenant and must be paid in cash or credited toward rent on the lease renewal or anniversary, or on January 31 if the tenant received written notice that payment will be made annually on that date.

Within 30 days after the tenancy ends, the landlord must return the security deposit plus interest earned, less lawful deductions. Any deductions require an itemized list sent to the tenant by registered or certified mail within that 30-day period.

Within five business days after a tenant is displaced by fire, flood, condemnation, or evacuation, the landlord must return the security deposit if an authorized public official has posted a notice prohibiting occupancy or certified that displacement is expected to last longer than seven days. The landlord must tell the tenant within three business days after receiving notice where the deposit can be collected.

New Jersey has no statewide rent-control limit. A landlord cannot increase rent during a lease term; to impose an increase after the lease ends, the landlord must give proper written notice and the increase must not be unconscionable or violate applicable municipal rent-control ordinances.
A landlord may charge a prospective tenant the cost of a credit report and may request reasonable rental application fees or employment verification.

The Act also restricts discriminatory statements, inquiries, and use or dissemination of an applicant’s criminal record.
A housing provider may not require an applicant to submit to a drug or alcohol test or request consent to obtain information from a drug abuse treatment facility.

After finding that a housing provider violated the act, the director may require the provider to return the applicant’s rental application fee, unless housing is provided to the applicant under paragraph (2).
A landlord may not evict a tenant solely because the lease term has ended.

When a tenant terminates a lease under the Safe Housing Act, the landlord must make the security deposit and interest available within 15 business days after termination. The landlord must notify the tenant in writing within three business days of when and where to collect it, and keep it available for 30 days. Any deductions must be itemized.
A landlord may not collect a security deposit exceeding one and one-half times one month’s rent. A pet security deposit counts toward that combined limit.
Any additional yearly security deposit increase may not exceed 10% of the current security deposit.

Interest or earnings on the security deposit belong to the tenant and must be paid in cash or credited toward rent on the lease renewal or anniversary, or on January 31 if the tenant received written notice that payment will be made annually on that date.

Within 30 days after the tenancy ends, the landlord must return the security deposit plus interest earned, less lawful deductions. Any deductions require an itemized list sent to the tenant by registered or certified mail within that 30-day period.

Within five business days after a tenant is displaced by fire, flood, condemnation, or evacuation, the landlord must return the security deposit if an authorized public official has posted a notice prohibiting occupancy or certified that displacement is expected to last longer than seven days. The landlord must tell the tenant within three business days after receiving notice where the deposit can be collected.
A landlord may charge a prospective tenant the cost of a credit report and may request reasonable rental application fees or employment verification.

A0499.explanation: The screening fee is capped at $68.96 for 2026. Landlords must provide a copy of a consumer credit report within 7 days of receipt, a receipt and itemized accounting of screening costs, and a refund of any unused portion of the fee.
If a tenant provides a reusable screening report, the landlord must use it.

A landlord cannot charge a screening fee when no rental unit is available. The landlord must return the fee to an applicant not selected, unless the landlord follows the stated application-order and no-charge-for-unconsidered-applicants policy.

Starting July 1, 2024, many landlords may charge no more than one month’s rent for furnished or unfurnished units. Landlords meeting the stated small-owner and ownership conditions may charge up to two months’ rent.
Last month’s rent is considered part of the security deposit; first month’s rent is not.
For a tenancy beginning on or after July 1, 2025, the landlord must photograph the unit immediately before or at the start of the tenancy to document its condition.
The landlord must offer a walk-through inspection during the last two weeks of a tenancy to identify items needing repair or cleaning.

A landlord may deduct only amounts reasonably necessary for rent default, tenant- or guest-caused damage beyond normal wear and tear, qualifying cleaning, and—if allowed by the lease—restoring or replacing personal property or furniture, excluding ordinary wear and tear.

A landlord may not require payment for, or claim against the tenant or deposit for, professional carpet cleaning or other professional cleaning unless reasonably necessary to return the premises to its starting condition, minus ordinary wear and tear.

The landlord must return the deposit or remaining portion within 21 days after the tenant leaves the unit vacant. If deductions are made, the landlord must provide a written itemized statement and supporting documents for repair or cleaning charges; starting January 1, 2025, the landlord must also provide proof that necessary repairs were completed.

Starting April 1, 2025, the landlord must photograph the unit after regaining possession but before repairs or cleaning for which a deposit deduction is intended. The photographs and a written explanation of the cost must be provided to the tenant with the itemized statement.
Housing providers may not charge households with children a higher security deposit as a discriminatory condition or rule.
Tenant screening, including screening conducted by a third party, may not discriminate based on a protected characteristic.

Housing providers may not discriminate against applicants or tenants based on their source of income, including by applying different tenancy terms or charging a higher security deposit because of that source.

Housing providers may not consider arrests that did not lead to conviction, sealed or expunged records, or juvenile-system matters, and may not impose blanket bans on people with criminal history. A conviction used to deny an application must be directly related to the applicant’s ability to be a good tenant and not threaten health, safety, or property; consider the crime’s nature and severity and time elapsed.

Prohibits using or distributing a common pricing algorithm as part of a contract, combination, or conspiracy to restrain trade or commerce, and prohibits using or distributing one to coerce another person to set or adopt its recommended price or commercial term.

For residential property used as the tenant’s dwelling, a landlord generally may not demand or receive security exceeding one month’s rent, in addition to first-month rent. A qualifying small landlord may demand up to two months’ rent, subject to the service-member limitation. An advance payment of at least six months’ rent is permitted when the lease term is six months or longer.

If a landlord or agent charges a service member higher-than-standard or higher-than-advertised security because of credit history, credit score, housing history, or another tenant-related factor, the landlord must provide a written statement of the amount and reason by the lease-signing date. The additional security must be returned after no more than six months of residency if the tenant is not in arrears for rent during that period, and the lease must state the return date.

A landlord may claim from security only amounts reasonably necessary for the purposes specified in subdivision (b). The landlord may not charge for preexisting damage or defective conditions, ordinary wear and tear, or professional cleaning unless reasonably necessary to return the premises to their inception-of-tenancy condition, excluding ordinary wear and tear.

After notice of an intention to terminate the tenancy or before the lease ends, the landlord must notify the tenant in writing of the option to request an initial inspection and the right to attend. If requested, the landlord must conduct the inspection at a reasonable time no earlier than two weeks before termination or lease end, and provide an itemized statement of proposed repair or cleaning deductions.
For tenancies that begin on or after July 1, 2025, the landlord must take photographs of the unit immediately before or at the inception of the tenancy.

Beginning April 1, 2025, the landlord must photograph the unit within a reasonable time after possession is returned and before repairs or cleaning for which a security deduction or claim will be made, and again within a reasonable time after those repairs or cleaning are completed.

No later than 21 calendar days after the tenant vacates, the landlord must provide an itemized statement of the basis for and amount of security received and its disposition, and return any remaining security, subject to the section’s timing and return-method provisions.
Security must be held by the landlord for the tenant who is party to the lease or agreement, and the tenant’s claim to the security takes priority over claims of the landlord’s creditors.

When deducting for repairs or cleaning, a landlord generally must provide supporting documentation with the itemized statement. If the work is done by the landlord or an employee, the statement must describe the work, time spent, and reasonable hourly rate. For work performed by others, the landlord must provide the bill, invoice, or receipt and, when needed, the provider’s contact information. Material costs and applicable photographs and cost explanations must also be provided. A good-faith estimate may be used in specified circumstances, with follow-up documentation due within 14 calendar days after the repair is completed or documentation is received.

When a landlord’s interest in the premises terminates, the landlord or agent must within a reasonable time either transfer the remaining security, after lawful deductions, to the successor in interest and notify the tenant of the transfer and relevant details, or return the remaining security to the tenant with an accounting. Before a voluntary transfer, the landlord must provide the successor a written statement of the remaining security, deductions, and election.

A lease or rental agreement may not characterize security as nonrefundable. Bad-faith claiming or retaining security in violation of the section, or bad-faith demand for replacement security in violation of the section, may result in statutory damages of up to twice the security amount in addition to actual damages.

A landlord may charge an application screening fee only up to the actual out-of-pocket costs and reasonable value of time spent obtaining applicant information, and the fee may not exceed $30 per applicant, subject to annual CPI adjustment.

A landlord may not charge an application screening fee when they know or should know that no rental unit is available now or within a reasonable time. A fee may be charged only when the landlord offers a qualifying screening process: completed applications considered in received order under written criteria, with the first applicant meeting those criteria approved and fees charged only when an application is considered; or the entire fee is returned to applicants not selected within the specified deadline. The landlord must provide an itemized receipt and return any unused portion of the fee when specified screening services are not performed.

A housing provider may not use a financial or income standard that fails to count the aggregate income of people residing or proposing to reside together on the same basis as the aggregate income of married people living together.

A landlord may terminate a covered tenancy only for a just cause reason. The listed reasons include specified tenant-fault causes and no-fault causes; relocation assistance may be required for no-fault evictions.
A landlord may not evict a tenant for falling behind on rent unless the amount owed is higher than the applicable Fair Market Rent (FMR), which depends on the unit's bedroom size.
For rental units subject to the RSO, rent may be increased once every 12 months, by the allowable rent-increase percentage.

A landlord may increase rent by 10% for an additional tenant who is not a dependent and moves into the rental unit. The increase must be made within 60 days of the landlord learning about the additional tenant.
Landlords may no longer add a 10% rent increase for an additional dependent added to the tenancy.
Landlords may no longer include an additional percentage increase for utilities.
Rent may be increased to the market rate if the tenant voluntarily moves out or is evicted for one of the listed reasons, or accepts a Tenant Buyout Agreement.

The document lists at-fault reasons including failure to pay rent, rental-agreement violations, nuisance or damage, illegal use, failure to renew a similar agreement, denial of reasonable access, and an unapproved subtenant at the end of the lease. It also lists no-fault reasons including owner or immediate-family move-in, resident-manager move-in, demolition and permanent removal from the rental market, government order, and conversion to affordable housing. No-fault evictions require relocation assistance.
Beginning February 2, 2026, landlords may not include an additional percentage increase for utilities.
Landlords may pass through the RSO and SCEP surcharges with proper written notice; the surcharges may be collected only after the landlord registers the units and gives written notice to the tenant.

For covered RSO or JCO units, landlords must pay relocation assistance and file a Declaration of Intent to Evict with LAHD before evicting tenants in a no-fault eviction. A termination notice may be served only after filing the declaration, and a copy of the notice must be filed with LAHD within 3 days after service.

A landlord terminating a tenancy to demolish a Protected Unit for new construction must file the applicable eviction or withdrawal notice with LAHD, serve tenants written notice and file a copy within 3 business days, and pay relocation assistance under state or city law, whichever is higher. City relocation amounts must be enhanced for lower-income tenants when required by the RPO or HCA.
